newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dlr ends at 65 U.S. cents, further selling seen.
newsitem.headline: NZ dlr ends at 65 U.S. cents, further selling seen.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar closed over one U.S. cent lower on Friday from its local close on Thursday and, though it stabilised in afternoon trade at 65 U.S. cents, dealers said its downward spiral was by no means over.
"There still seems to be selling interest from offshore, I expect it to go lower," said a bank chief dealer, adding that charts indicated a target of US$0.6250.
The Kiwi closed at US$0.6494/01 and at 64.47 on its Trade-Weighted Index. It opened at US$6547/54 at 65.05 on the TWI, having shed half a cent overnight from its 0.6600/07 local close on Thursday.

"We've seen some medium-term guys hedging their positions, we've seen some outright sellers out of the States, even the guys out of Hong Kong have been selling it, and they've been long for years," said a dealer.

While interest rates shot skyward to offset the weaknening currency's affect on monetary conditions, dealers said the increasingly attractive rates were unlikely to garner support for the kiwi in the short term.
"At the end of the day I think it's just a general disinvestment, which means interest rates are really irrelevant to the equation," said the chief dealer.
"It's only people selling out of long positions, it's not people getting short, so higher interest rates don't really affect their equation.
"That's why you're not seeing any support coming in as the interest rates go up.
"It's fine to get the extra two or three percent on your investment, but what happens if the currency goes down three big figures?
"People won't get into it while there's a perception that the exchange rate will go lower -- it just isn't worth it," he said.

Dealers said the Reserve Bank would not be unhappy with the change in the mix of monetary conditions, which are now as close to the bank's comfort zone as they have been at any time since its last major policy statement in late June.
The Monetary Conditions Index closed at 770 -- 55 points below the RBNZ's desired level of 825 in the September quarter, but only five points outside its 50-point comfort zone.

"I think the Reserve Bank will be reasonably happy with the mix. Their only worry has been inflation in the housing market, and these higher interest rates should knock that out," said the chief dealer.

The kiwi was seen trading in a 0.6450-6510 range, although dealers said the volatility of the currency made it hard to forecast a range. It was generally expected to come under further selling pressure in New York, they said.
